pos: n. pl. (the family descended from Ard, grandson of Benjamin; named once)
etymology: Patronymic plural from Ard, Hebrew 'Ard, probably a fugitive or one who descends; the family registered in the second wilderness census, Numbers 26:40.
biblical_def: The Ardites are named once, in the Benjamite section of the census taken on the plains of Moab: “And the sons of Bela were Ard and Naaman: of Ard, the family of the Ardites: and of Naaman, the family of the Naamites” (Numbers 26:40). Ard is listed among the sons of Benjamin who went down into Egypt — “And the sons of Benjamin were Belah, and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, Ehi, and Rosh, Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard” (Genesis 46:21) — and here appears as a son of Bela, which is the ordinary looseness of Hebrew sonship, where son may mean grandson or descendant. The tribe's total follows: “These are the sons of Benjamin after their families: and they that were numbered of them were forty and five thousand and six hundred” (Numbers 26:41). The purpose of the whole register was given at its head: “Take the sum of all the congregation of the children of Israel, from twenty years old and upward, throughout their fathers' house, all that are able to go to war in Israel” (Numbers 26:2). A family name in this chapter is therefore a muster-roll entry and a deed of inheritance at once. God counted Israel by households, and the Ardites were a household He counted.

corruption_summary: The genealogies are dismissed as tribal propaganda, where Numbers 26 is a legal register on which an inheritance and a military obligation both depended.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard critical treatment of a list like this is that it is late invention, drawn up to legitimate claims after the fact. The chapter's own structure tells against the charge. It is a census of fighting men by household, taken for two stated purposes: to know who could go to war, and to apportion the land “according to the number of names.” Lists made to flatter do not fix obligations; they do not record small families alongside large; and they do not, as this chapter does, conclude by naming the whole generation that died under judgment.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God deals with men in families. The Ardites are one line in a register, but the register is the reason Benjamin had a portion and the reason Benjamin had a muster. A household name in Scripture is never merely sentimental; it carries duty and inheritance together.

pos: n. pl. (the family descended from Areli, son of Gad; named once)
etymology: Patronymic plural from Areli, Hebrew 'Ar'eli, commonly explained as lion of God or heroic; registered in the census of Numbers 26:17.
biblical_def: The Arelites close the roll of Gad's families: “Of Arod, the family of the Arodites: of Areli, the family of the Arelites” (Numbers 26:17). Areli himself is named among the sons who went down into Egypt with Jacob: “And the sons of Gad; Ziphion, and Haggi, Shuni, and Ezbon, Eri, and Arodi, and Areli” (Genesis 46:16). The seven names of that verse become the seven families of Numbers 26, and the tribe's number follows: “These are the families of the children of Gad according to those that were numbered of them, forty thousand and five hundred” (Numbers 26:18). Gad's position in that generation is worth noting. It was Gad and Reuben who asked for the land east of Jordan because they had much cattle, and who were required to cross over armed and fight until their brethren had rest before returning to it. The census that lists the Arelites is the census of the men who made that bargain and kept it. The chapter ends with the land ordered by the same lists: “Unto these the land shall be divided for an inheritance according to the number of names” (Numbers 26:53).

corruption_summary: Tribal registers are read as fiction because they are tidy, where their function was to bind men to an inheritance they had to fight for first.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 26 is often treated as an idealized scheme rather than a record, on the ground that genealogies are too orderly to be real. The order is the point: a register made for dividing land has to be orderly or it is useless. And the chapter is not flattering. Gad numbers forty thousand five hundred, fewer than at the first census; several tribes shrank; the whole generation first numbered had died in the wilderness. A fiction composed to glorify the tribes would not have recorded the losses.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Gad was taught by its own request. The tribe wanted the near country and was granted it on condition of crossing Jordan armed and staying until the last tribe had rest. Inheritance and duty come together in Scripture, and the family names were written down in the same chapter as the muster.

pos: n. pl. (the family descended from Hamul, son of Pharez; named once)
etymology: Patronymic plural from Hamul, Hebrew Chamul, pitied or spared, from chamal, to spare or have compassion; registered at Numbers 26:21.
biblical_def: The Hamulites are named once: “And the sons of Pharez were; of Hezron, the family of the Hezronites: of Hamul, the family of the Hamulites” (Numbers 26:21). Hamul was one of the two sons of Pharez, and Pharez was one of the twins born to Judah by Tamar, so that the line stands in a genealogy Scripture reports without excuse: “And the sons of Judah; Er, and Onan, and Shelah, and Pharez, and Zerah: but Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan. And the sons of Pharez were Hezron and Hamul” (Genesis 46:12). Chronicles repeats the pair in four words: “The sons of Pharez; Hezron, and Hamul” (1 Chronicles 2:5). The name itself is a mercy: Hamul means pitied, or spared. He is Judah's grandson by a shameful episode, born into the tribe that would carry the sceptre, and the brother line through Hezron runs on to Boaz, to Jesse, to David, and to Christ. The whole register exists to fix an inheritance: “Unto these the land shall be divided for an inheritance according to the number of names” (Numbers 26:53). The Hamulites had a portion in Judah because a man named Pitied had a son.

corruption_summary: The irregularities in Judah's line are treated as evidence against the Bible's moral seriousness, where Scripture reports them and carries the promise through them.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite misreadings meet at this family. One takes Judah and Tamar as proof that Scripture is indifferent to sin, since the line of promise runs through that episode. The other is embarrassed and quietly skips the chapter. Scripture does neither. Genesis names the sin as sin, records that Er and Onan died under judgment, and then keeps the register honest. The gospel is not that God found a clean family, but that He kept His word through an unclean one without ever calling the uncleanness good.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the name. Hamul means spared, and he is a son of the house of Judah by Tamar — which is to say that the sparing began long before anyone deserved it, and that sovereign mercy is the only reason there is a tribe here to number at all.

pos: n. pl. (the family descended from Hupham of Benjamin; named once)
etymology: Patronymic plural from Hupham, Hebrew Chupham, a coast-dweller or one protected; registered among the Benjamite families at Numbers 26:39.
biblical_def: The Huphamites are named once: “Of Shupham, the family of the Shuphamites: of Hupham, the family of the Huphamites” (Numbers 26:39). The Benjamite list of Genesis 46 has Muppim and Huppim where Numbers has Shupham and Hupham — “And the sons of Benjamin were Belah, and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, Ehi, and Rosh, Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard” (Genesis 46:21) — and the dictionary notes the variation without pretending to resolve what Scripture leaves. The Authorized Version renders each book as it stands. The tribal total follows in the next verses: “These are the sons of Benjamin after their families: and they that were numbered of them were forty and five thousand and six hundred” (Numbers 26:41). Benjamin is the youngest tribe and the one that would later be nearly destroyed in a civil war and then rebuilt; it would give Israel its first king and the church its apostle to the Gentiles. In this chapter it is simply a list of households able to bear arms, counted by name: “Take the sum of all the congregation of the children of Israel, from twenty years old and upward” (Numbers 26:2).

corruption_summary: Variant spellings between parallel lists are urged as proof of a corrupted text, where the Authorized Version renders each book faithfully and the variation is ordinary.
corruption_paragraphs: Hupham and Huppim, Shupham and Muppim, are a favourite exhibit in arguments that the Hebrew text is unreliable. The argument proves less than it claims. Variant forms of the same personal name are common in every language and were common in Hebrew, where several letters are close in form; a man may also be known by more than one name, as Scripture shows repeatedly. What a faithful translation owes the reader is to render what each book actually has, and to let the reader see the difference — which is exactly what the Authorized Version does here.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the preservation of Scripture is a doctrine about the text God has given, not a promise that every parallel list will be harmonized for our convenience. The register did its work: Benjamin was mustered and Benjamin received a portion, and the families were counted one by one.

pos: n. pl. (the family descended from Hanoch, eldest son of Reuben; named once)
etymology: Patronymic plural from Hanoch, Hebrew Chanok, dedicated or initiated, the same name borne by the patriarch Enoch; registered at Numbers 26:5.
biblical_def: The Hanochites stand at the head of the whole census, because Reuben was Jacob's firstborn: “Reuben, the eldest son of Israel: the children of Reuben; Hanoch, of whom cometh the family of the Hanochites: of Pallu, the family of the Palluites” (Numbers 26:5). Hanoch is the first of the four sons Reuben brought into Egypt: “And the sons of Reuben; Hanoch, and Phallu, and Hezron, and Carmi” (Genesis 46:9). The tribe's number closes the section: “These are the families of the Reubenites: and they that were numbered of them were forty and three thousand and seven hundred and thirty” (Numbers 26:7). Reuben's place in the list is instructive. He was the firstborn and lost the pre-eminence of the firstborn by his own sin; the sceptre went to Judah and the double portion to Joseph, and yet Reuben is still numbered first, still given a portion, still called the eldest son of Israel. The chapter also records what the generation before had come to: “For the LORD had said of them, They shall surely die in the wilderness. And there was not left a man of them, save Caleb the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua the son of Nun” (Numbers 26:65).

corruption_summary: Birth order is treated as the Bible's rule of blessing, where Reuben's case shows the firstborn forfeiting pre-eminence while keeping his place in the family.
corruption_paragraphs: It is often said that Scripture simply privileges the firstborn, and that its blessings follow blood and birth order mechanically. The firstborn of Israel is a standing refutation. Reuben's sin at his father's bed cost him the pre-eminence; Jacob's blessing says so plainly; and the kingly line went to the fourth son and the double portion to the eleventh. God is not bound by human precedence, and He says so by the very order of a census that still lists Reuben first.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the severity and the kindness together. Reuben lost what could not be recovered and was not cast off; the Hanochites were numbered, and had their inheritance, and were called the children of the eldest son of Israel. Discipline in the covenant is real, and it is not rejection.

pos: n. pl. (the family descended from Haggi, son of Gad; named once)
etymology: Patronymic plural from Haggi, Hebrew Chaggi, festive or born on a feast day, from chag, a feast; registered at Numbers 26:15.
biblical_def: The Haggites are named once, in the Gadite roll: “The children of Gad after their families: of Zephon, the family of the Zephonites: of Haggi, the family of the Haggites: of Shuni, the family of the Shunites” (Numbers 26:15). Haggi is the second son named in Gad's household at the descent into Egypt: “And the sons of Gad; Ziphion, and Haggi, Shuni, and Ezbon, Eri, and Arodi, and Areli” (Genesis 46:16). The tribe's total is given four verses later: “These are the families of the children of Gad according to those that were numbered of them, forty thousand and five hundred” (Numbers 26:18). The name is worth a moment. Chaggi is built on chag, the word for a pilgrim feast — Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles — and it is the same root behind the prophet Haggai's name. A child called Festive was most likely born at one of the appointed times, which means the family name itself is a small witness that Israel in Egypt still kept count of the calendar of God. The register of the land follows the same households: “Notwithstanding the land shall be divided by lot: according to the names of the tribes of their fathers they shall inherit” (Numbers 26:55).

corruption_summary: The feasts are presented as borrowed agricultural festivals, where Scripture appoints them, dates them and attaches them to acts of redemption.
corruption_paragraphs: Because the appointed feasts fall at harvest seasons, it is commonly asserted that Israel took over Canaanite agricultural festivals and attached national stories to them afterwards. The order in Scripture is the reverse. The first feast was instituted in Egypt, before there was a harvest or a land, and its subject was a lamb and a doorpost. The feasts are tied to events — the exodus, the giving of the law, the wilderness tents — and the agricultural calendar was made to serve them. A name like Haggi, carried out of Egypt, is a quiet witness that the calendar came first.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the feasts were shadows of a substance. Christ is our passover; the firstfruits are His resurrection; the Spirit came at Pentecost. A family called Festive in the second generation out of Egypt was carrying a word whose fulfilment was still fifteen centuries off.

pos: n. pl. (the family descended from Guni, son of Naphtali; named once)
etymology: Patronymic plural from Guni, Hebrew Guni, commonly explained as protected or painted; registered among the families of Naphtali at Numbers 26:48.
biblical_def: The Gunites are named once, in the last tribal section of the census: “Of the sons of Naphtali after their families: of Jahzeel, the family of the Jahzeelites: of Guni, the family of the Gunites” (Numbers 26:48). Guni is the second of the four sons of Naphtali who went down into Egypt: “And the sons of Naphtali; Jahzeel, and Guni, and Jezer, and Shillem” (Genesis 46:24). The tribe's number closes the roll: “These are the families of Naphtali according to their families: and they that were numbered of them were forty and five thousand and four hundred” (Numbers 26:50). Naphtali was a northern tribe, settled in the hill country west of the sea of Chinnereth, and its territory would afterwards be called Galilee. It was among the first carried away by Assyria, and Isaiah named it as the first to see the light: the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, where the great light shined and where Christ Himself afterwards dwelt and preached. The register that counted the Gunites is therefore the beginning of a long account, and it ends where the chapter says it must: “Unto these the land shall be divided for an inheritance according to the number of names” (Numbers 26:53).

corruption_summary: The tribal allotments are treated as politics projected backwards, where Scripture fixes them before the land is entered and ties them to a promise.
corruption_paragraphs: The account of tribal territories is commonly explained as a later settlement written back into Moses' mouth. Numbers 26 makes an awkward witness for that reading. The register is taken while Israel is still on the plains of Moab with nothing yet in hand; the method of division is fixed in advance, by number and by lot; and the lot is expressly said to belong to the LORD. A document composed after the fact to justify what the tribes had seized would not stake everything on a method that nobody could manipulate.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reach of the promise. Naphtali is a name in a wilderness census here, and seven centuries later Isaiah says the light would dawn in its borders, and seven centuries after that the Lord Jesus walked there. God counts households before He fulfils prophecies, and He does not lose the thread between them.

pos: n. pl. (a family name borne in two distinct tribes, Reuben and Judah; named twice)
etymology: Patronymic plural from Hezron, Hebrew Chetsron, enclosed or of an enclosure, from chatser, a court or village; registered twice in Numbers 26.
biblical_def: The Hezronites are named twice in one chapter, and the two are not the same family. The first stands in Reuben's line: “Of Hezron, the family of the Hezronites: of Carmi, the family of the Carmites” (Numbers 26:6), answering to the four sons of Reuben named in Egypt, “Hanoch, and Phallu, and Hezron, and Carmi” (Genesis 46:9). The second stands in Judah's: “And the sons of Pharez were; of Hezron, the family of the Hezronites: of Hamul, the family of the Hamulites” (Numbers 26:21). Two men bore the name, in different tribes, and each left a family that carried it; the Authorized Version keeps both, and a reader who assumes one family will misread the chapter. The second is the line that matters most for the whole of Scripture, for it is this Hezron, son of Pharez, from whom Ram and Amminadab and Nahshon and Boaz descend, and so Jesse and David, and so Christ according to the flesh. Chronicles sets the pair down plainly: “The sons of Pharez; Hezron, and Hamul” (1 Chronicles 2:5). A name repeated in two tribes is an ordinary thing in Israel, and in this instance one of the two is the royal line.

corruption_summary: A name occurring twice in one chapter is taken for a copyist's duplication, where Scripture is distinguishing two families in two tribes.
corruption_paragraphs: The repetition of Hezronites within fifteen verses is sometimes offered as a scribal error or a sign of composite sources. The text itself removes the difficulty. The first Hezron is set among Reuben's sons and paired with Carmi; the second is set among the sons of Pharez and paired with Hamul; and Genesis and Chronicles independently confirm both households. Shared personal names across tribes are everywhere in Scripture, as they are in every nation, and the careful reader is helped rather than hindered by a version that renders each occurrence as it stands.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the care Scripture takes with the line of promise. The Judahite Hezron is a link in the chain that runs from Pharez to Boaz to David to Christ, and the Holy Ghost preserved him in a wilderness muster-roll, in a Chronicler's register, and in the first chapter of Matthew.

pos: n. pl. (the family descended from Ahiram of Benjamin; named once)
etymology: Patronymic plural from Ahiram, Hebrew 'Achiram, brother of height, that is, exalted brother, from 'ach, a brother, and rum, to be high; registered at Numbers 26:38.
biblical_def: The Ahiramites are named once: “The sons of Benjamin after their families: of Bela, the family of the Belaites: of Ashbel, the family of the Ashbelites: of Ahiram, the family of the Ahiramites” (Numbers 26:38). The Benjamite list of Genesis names Ehi where Numbers has Ahiram — “And the sons of Benjamin were Belah, and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, Ehi, and Rosh, Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard” (Genesis 46:21) — and Chronicles has Aher in a Benjamite register; the forms stand in the text and the Authorized Version renders each as it is. The tribe is counted in the next verses: “These are the sons of Benjamin after their families: and they that were numbered of them were forty and five thousand and six hundred” (Numbers 26:41). The name means exalted brother, and it belongs to the tribe that would be brought lowest of all. After the outrage at Gibeah, Benjamin was reduced to six hundred men; the other tribes wept and then provided for the remnant, and the tribe was rebuilt from almost nothing. The register that counts forty-five thousand six hundred Benjamites was taken before any of that, when the land was still a promise: “Unto these the land shall be divided for an inheritance according to the number of names” (Numbers 26:53).

corruption_summary: Benjamin's near destruction is read as tribal myth, where Judges records it as judgment on Israel's own sin and Scripture keeps the tribe alive by mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: The history of Benjamin is treated by critical readers as an etiological legend explaining why a small tribe was small. The account in Judges does not read like an explanation anyone would invent. It records a crime inside Israel, a civil war the other tribes nearly lost twice before winning, a rash oath that made the victors' mercy awkward, and a remnant of six hundred men. The chapter that ends it says that in those days there was no king in Israel and every man did what was right in his own eyes — which is a verdict on the narrator's own people, not a boast.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God preserves what He has promised through judgment rather than around it. The exalted brother's family was numbered among forty-five thousand, cut down to six hundred, and restored; and out of restored Benjamin came Saul the king and Saul of Tarsus the apostle.

pos: n. pl. (the Manassite family of Abiezer, to which Gideon belonged; named twice)
etymology: Patronymic plural from Abiezer, Hebrew 'Abi'ezer, my father is help, from 'ab, a father, and 'ezer, help; the family of Ophrah in Manasseh, Judges 6:24 and 8:32.
biblical_def: The Abiezrites are the family of Gideon, and both occurrences name their town: “Then Gideon built an altar there unto the LORD, and called it Jehovahshalom: unto this day it is yet in Ophrah of the Abiezrites” (Judges 6:24), and at the end of his life, “And Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age, and was buried in the sepulchre of Joash his father, in Ophrah of the Abiezrites” (Judges 8:32). The singular form appears when the angel first comes: “And there came an angel of the LORD, and sat under an oak which was in Ophrah, that pertained unto Joash the Abiezrite: and his son Gideon threshed wheat by the winepress, to hide it from the Midianites” (Judges 6:11). The detail in that verse is the measure of the hour: a man of Israel threshing in hiding, by a winepress, because Midian took everything that stood in the open. Gideon's own estimate of his family was the lowest possible — his was the poor household in the least tribe — and the answer given him was that the LORD would be with him. The name he gave the altar, which the Authorized Version's margin renders “The LORD send peace,” was given before a single Midianite had fallen.

corruption_summary: Gideon is made a model of self-discovery and latent courage, where Judges insists the deliverance was God's and reduced his army to prove it.
corruption_paragraphs: Gideon is the favourite text of a therapeutic preaching that finds in him a man with hidden potential who needed only to believe in himself. The chapter resists it at every turn. He is found hiding; he asks for signs; he pleads his family's poverty; and when he raises an army of thirty-two thousand God cuts it to three hundred for a reason stated outright, lest Israel vaunt itself and say its own hand had saved it. The narrative is constructed to remove every ground of self-confidence, and the altar is named for peace from God before any victory.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the family name itself: my father is help. Gideon's town was called by a name that confessed where help came from, and the judge who came out of it was taught the same lesson by a shrinking army and a jar and a trumpet.
